label: Section heading
text: Licensing is the other axis
context: New section on /trust/, after placement. Introduces the five licence classes.

label: Standfirst
text: A trust class says what a host can see. A licence class says what a customer can do with the code. CARLOS dictates neither; it asks you to name both.

label: L1 name
text: Libre

label: L1 description
text: Free as in freedom and free of charge. Anyone may run, change and redistribute it. The operator earns from hosting or support, or not at all.
context: Examples shown beneath: amadan, the framework and this site.

label: L2 name
text: Source-available, commercial

label: L2 description
text: You can read it and self-host it; commercial use or redistribution needs a licence from the author.
context: Examples: Slopbox; Eleven as intended. Note: Eleven's repository carries MPL-2.0 today, which is libre, so the page says 'as intended'.

label: L3 name
text: Open source, with a hosted offering

label: L3 description
text: Fully open, and the author also runs it for you. The hosted service is the product; the code is the guarantee you can leave.
context: Example: Oficina, as intended (no licence file yet).

label: L4 name
text: Closed source, hosted only

label: L4 description
text: The author runs it and does not ship the code. Ownership for the customer means their instance, their data and their trust class, not the binary.
context: Example: a conventional SaaS moving onto CARLOS. Tony's app, unnamed.

label: L5 name
text: Closed source, hosted and on-prem

label: L5 description
text: The author ships a binary the customer may run on their own boxes under licence, and also hosts it. One codebase, every deployment mode.
context: Examples: Tito; Jelly, in development.

label: Closing note
text: The two axes are independent. An L5 app can be class A; an L1 app can be class C. A gallery entry names both, or says which has not been published yet.

label: Section heading
text: Remixability is the third
context: Third section on /trust/, after licensing.

label: Standfirst
text: Trust says what a host can see. Licence says what a customer may do. Remixability says what an agent, or a person with a fork, can actually do today. Three flags, each yes or no.

label: Flag 1 name
text: Forkable
context: Shown as R·fork.

label: Flag 1 description
text: The source is available and a fork that stays close to upstream keeps working with the shared glue: sign-on, the edge, hibernation, the trust class. Drift far enough and you are on your own, which is fair.
context: Example line beneath: follows from the licence, L1 to L3 yes, L4 and L5 no.

label: Flag 2 name
text: Agent-driveable
context: R·drive.

label: Flag 2 description
text: The app opts actions in as typed tools, so an agent reaches the same handler a person does, through the same middleware, with a confirmation sentence on every write. The framework provides this; the app has to switch it on.
context: Example line: the model supports it; no app has published tools yet. Verified today: no app in the family declares a rastrillo Tool.

label: Flag 3 name
text: Agent-rebuildable
context: R·build.

label: Flag 3 description
text: The app publishes a skill at its well-known URL, so an agent can fork it, change it and redeploy it without a person reading the code first. The framework publishes two skills; each app owes its own.
context: Example line: the model supports it; no app has published a skill yet. Verified today: keymail.dev, amadan.net, woodstar.app and oficina.works all 404 on /.well-known/agent-skills/.

label: Closing note
text: All three are possible for every app in the family, because every app has the same shape. The gallery records which ones have done it, not which ones could.

label: Standfirst (revised again)
text: Every app carries a trust class, S to C, a licence class, L1 to L5, and three remix flags. Publish the database and see what leaks.
context: Replaces the earlier revision; now names all three axes.
